doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Self-taught arranger and piano; Dino Govoni's remark
summary: He was a slow, self-taught arranger and plays piano like a little kid with crab fingers, per Dino Govoni.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Not the arranging, I was slow. I was a slow arranger. Dick went to Manhattan School of Music. I’m very close with Dick. And he’s a great arranger by the way. I spoke to him some years ago and I said, we were just talking and I said, “I was slow. I went to Berklee a couple of months and I left.” You know so I wrote one chart, “There Will Never Be Another You.” Just straight through, like a little drop two harmony, drop, whatever it

was. Most — I’m a self-taught arranger. And I’m self-taught on the piano. I feel like a little kid. You know Dino Govoni who teaches, he’s a very good saxophone player across the hall from me at Berklee. I played piano once in his room, I was trying out the piano in his room. We all have pianos. And I played for about twenty minutes. He was smiling. He says, “Fred, when you play you’re like a little kid.” He said, and he loves me on saxophone, alto or tenor. He says, “If I could play piano like you I’d give up my saxophone.” I was crying you know. He’s looking at me, like he was smiling, just like an innocent little kid. He says — and I’ve had other people say that. I don’t — I can’t look at myself and I’m not — I’m just, it’s just very natural. I play totally incorrect, Mozart fingering no. I play like a crab. Crab fingers. Sometimes they get a voicing. But I’m very relaxed so I can play very fast. I can’t do what Chick and all the other people do, but I have my own style. No one sounds like me. It’s not bragging it’s just the way, from playing and playing and playing. That’s like what the guitar player we talked about, just keep doing it.

Find your thing. So I play a certain — I’m looking at my students, my saxophone students, “How do you play like that.” I said, “I just kept playing over the years.” And I’m talking and I go [scats] you know four octaves down on some kind of pentatonic thing. If it’s in my fingers, in the last ten years, I got it. And with weird, crab-like fingerings. And I’m looking. I’m just being silly.
Hey that’s okay. Thelonious Monk didn’t have the greatest hand technique, right?
